Air pollution may change the brain — but not the same way for everyone.

New USC research shows dirty air was linked to thinner brain tissue in 23 of 34 areas studied — beyond just Alzheimer's-related regions. In older women, more pollution was linked to a brain that looked older. In younger men, the pattern was different — and flipped around age 65.

This is not a personal risk score. It shows a pattern across many people — not a prediction for any one person.

Check your local air quality. Exercise outside when the air is cleaner.

If you carry APOE4, how much you move — and how long you sit — may shape your brain health long before memory symptoms begin.

Our team recently published an umbrella review on APOE4, physical activity, and brain health. The strongest signals came from studies of younger or cognitively healthy adults: physical activity was linked to better cognition, lower dementia risk, and healthier brain markers — sometimes more clearly in APOE4 carriers.

Why this matters for APOE4 carriers:
APOE4 is not only an Alzheimer's risk gene. It influences blood vessels, inflammation, and how the brain uses energy — systems that exercise can influence.

Research also shows that long sitting time matters on its own. In a large UK Biobank study, dementia risk began to rise after about 10 hours per day of sedentary time.

The encouraging part: the benefit is not linear. Moving from sedentary to somewhat active may matter more than going from active to perfectly optimized.

Practical first steps:
→ Stand and move for 2–5 minutes every 30–60 minutes
→ Take a 10-minute walk after meals
→ Track your baseline steps, then increase gradually
→ Build toward 150 minutes/week of moderate activity plus strength training

A morning workout helps — but it does not fully cancel 8–10 hours of uninterrupted sitting. For brain health, your daily movement pattern matters.

For APOE4 carriers, physical activity and sedentary time may influence brain health through vascular, metabolic, and inflammatory pathways — especially before symptoms begin.

At the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health, we connect basic science on neuroinflammation and genetic risk (including APOE4) with personalized prevention in our Prevention Clinic.

Dr. Hussein Yassine's recent overview highlights findings from our umbrella review:

• Physical activity linked to better cognition and lower dementia risk — benefits sometimes more pronounced in APOE4 carriers
• Inactive APOE4 carriers often face higher cognitive risk, pointing to modifiable factors
• Sedentary time matters independently: dementia risk rises after ~10 hours/day of sitting
• The largest gains may come from moving out of the lowest activity category

Exercise is not a guaranteed shield against Alzheimer's disease. But for APOE4 carriers, becoming someone who moves throughout the day may be one of the most rational places to start.
